absent: Full definitions of superblock, inode, dentry, writeback and backing device structures beyond fields observed in these fragments.
Mount, remount, unmount entry paths, filesystem type registration, sget lookup, kill_sb dispatch and put_super behavior.
Security, notification, encryption keyring and quota hook semantics beyond teardown invocation points.
Reclaim scan and count logic, LRU management, shrinker registration lifetime and memory cgroup interaction details.
Writeback worker execution, scheduling, bandwidth estimation updates and completion queue memory ordering beyond submission and wait.
Configuration conditions selecting alternate builds for page splitting, work fan out and switch semaphore handling.
Lockdep classes, global superblock list protection, nested subclass rules and freeze level ordering constraints.
Error code values, logging format strings and hung task timeout configuration beyond threshold based diagnostic presence.

findings.text: Filesystem error accounting exposes mount initialization and unmount drain around s_pending_errors. Mount biases the counter so waits only trigger during teardown, while unmount releases the bias and otherwise waits for the counter to fall below one.
Anonymous superblock teardown leaves the instance unusable for new acquisitions, ensures teardown observers have been notified, and returns the anonymous device number to the allocator.

General shutdown applies when a root exists and results in the superblock leaving active service, with cached namespace and inode state discarded, writeback and error tracking quiesced, optional filesystem and security teardown hooks invoked, dying visibility published to concurrent walkers, exclusive protection released, and backing device linkage reset to a neutral sink.

Dentry reclamation for unmount detaches the primary root and repeatedly reclaims secondary roots until none remain, dropping each tree and waiting for concurrent users of already dying entries where needed.
Cgroup writeback teardown is inert for backing devices without writeback capability and otherwise ensures in flight inode associations have drained after active service has ended.

Inode eviction for teardown selects only unreferenced and stable inodes, marks them to prevent new references, removes them from reclaim tracking, and then releases them outside global list protection with scheduling opportunities.

Filesystem synchronization is inert on read only instances and otherwise coordinates inode writeback, optional filesystem sync hooks in early and late modes, and block device synchronization, propagating the first failure encountered.

Inode synchronization for a superblock skips neutral backing devices, opportunistically kicks flushers without waiting when integrity is disabled, and otherwise issues a full range synchronous writeback barrier followed by a wait for in flight inodes under protection against writeback domain switches.
Opportunistic superblock writeback estimates dirty state volume from global counters and issues background work that is skipped for neutral or clean backing devices.
Writeback completion waiting drops the initial reference and sleeps until all queued work signals completion, emitting a diagnostic if the wait exceeds the configured hung task threshold.

Flusher wakeup traverses backing device writeback domains and requests background work only where dirty state exists, coalescing concurrent start all requests so at most one remains pending per domain.

Dirty inode estimation derives from the difference between total and unused inode counters summed across processors, clamped at zero to tolerate concurrent underflow, and combined with dirty page state for writeback sizing.
Filesystem context logging provides warning and error helpers that append formatted messages to the context log with distinct severity markers.

Deferred superblock destruction runs in workqueue context and fully releases an unregistered instance, covering memory, freeze protection, naming helpers, user namespace linkage, plus security and notification teardown.
Binfmt misc context wiring selects dedicated free and tree acquisition handlers, while its superblock teardown delegates to anonymous teardown and then releases the stored user namespace.

A freshly allocated superblock starts with biased passive and active references, neutral backing handling, caller flags with extra isolation for non initial user namespaces, default size and time settings with fallback operations, empty namespace and inode tracking with associated locks, per level freeze protection and held nested umount protection, plus attached reclaim, LRU and device helper state.
Superblock device helpers bind a device number to its owner with an initial single reference and zeroed remainder.

Background superblock writeback uses nonblocking mode with tagged page handling and a caller supplied page budget, while full synchronization uses blocking all range mode with cyclic disabled and a sync marker.
Writeback completions start with an initial reference that the waiter drops, with each queued item holding one reference that is released on finish and waking all waiters when the last one departs.

Page budget division across writeback domains is proportional to recent throughput with rounding up and conservative fallbacks for unbounded, zero total or dominant local cases in one build, and identity passthrough in the alternate build.
Protection against writeback domain switches during full sync is provided by a dedicated read write semaphore in one build and compiled to no ops in the alternate build.
Superblock notification teardown is an inert inline hook in the routed configuration.

Superblock acquisition forbids entry while umount protection is already held, succeeds only for born and nondying instances with the requested shared or exclusive protection held on return, and returns refusal without protection for dying instances including those that transition while waiting.

Temporary acquisition keeps the object alive with a passive hold across global list lock release, and on return either holds exclusive protection with validated active use or has waited for terminal visibility and released its hold while reporting failure.

Unmount time namespace and inode reclamation requires exclusive umount protection, serializes root hash access with a dedicated spinlock, serializes per dentry mutation with its own lock under RCU coverage, and serializes global inode walks with list and per inode locks while allowing rescheduling.
Writeback queueing and explicit wakeup serialize work list mutation and registration checks under interrupt safe work lock protection, promoting idle domains to active scheduling when registered.

Fan out of superblock work to multiple writeback domains iterates under RCU with per domain liveness pinning, queueing heap work when allocation succeeds and otherwise executing on stack fallback work synchronously with restart.

The superblock carries freeze and umount protection, user namespace linkage, flags and filesystem type linkage, root hash plus global and writeback inode lists with their locks, sync and rename serialization, backing device and block device linkage, operation vectors, size and time bounds, shrinker and LRU reclaim state, device helpers, error and writeback counters, plus workqueue and completion helpers observed across allocation, use and teardown.

Writeback work descriptors carry target superblock, sync mode, page budget, tagging and cyclic controls, reason and sync markers, completion linkage and lifetime flags, while completions carry a reference count, wait queue, timing and progress tracking.
Filesystem context operations wire free and tree acquisition handlers, and superblock device helpers pair a device number with its owner plus a reference count.

Superblock visibility progresses from unborn to born and active, then to dying broadcast with exclusive protection released, and finally to dead where new acquisitions fail and temporary holders are woken. Concurrent finders keep observing the object until the terminal mark while other walkers discard it once dying is visible.

Inodes become eligible for teardown eviction only when reference counts read zero at two checkpoints and none of I_WILL_FREE, I_FREEING and I_NEW are set. Selected inodes are marked freeing, detached from reclaim tracking, and released after list protection is dropped.
Per domain background start requests are coalesced by a test and set marker so concurrent triggers collapse into a single pending activation carrying the latest reason until the worker consumes it.

Failure to evict all inodes before final teardown is treated as data corruption, with continued operation poisoning inode operation, superblock and mapping linkages to force a clean failure on later access rather than silent use after teardown.

Teardown must not leak anonymous device numbers and must return backing linkage to a neutral sink, releasing per super backing registration where present, otherwise later allocations or writeback could act on stale associations.
Synchronization failures in filesystem hooks or block layer are propagated immediately without proceeding to later phases, preserving error visibility over best effort progress.
Fresh instances default s_time_gran to 1000000000, s_time_min to TIME64_MIN, s_time_max to TIME64_MAX, and s_maxbytes to MAX_NON_LFS.
Reclaim batching uses 1024 objects per scan and writeback uses MIN_WRITEBACK_PAGES as the minimum threshold, with shrinker names derived per filesystem type and NUMA plus memcg awareness enabled.
Freeze protection is replicated across SB_FREEZE_LEVELS with per level names from sb_writers_name and per type keys.

Lifecycle and behavior flags observed include SB_I_NO_DATA_INTEGRITY, SB_I_PERSB_BDI, SB_I_NODEV, SB_ACTIVE, SB_DEAD, SB_DYING and SB_BORN, plus WB_REASON_SYNC, WB_SYNC_ALL, WB_SYNC_NONE and BDI_CAP_WRITEBACK for writeback control.
